extracted.intended_audience: sellers offering negative-option features (subscription/auto-renewal businesses), compliance teams, and legal counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and binding requirements for sellers on cancellation, reminders, disclosures, exemptions, and related consumer-protection obligations under the FTC's negative-option final Rule. Focuses on how to provide and effectuate cancellations, timing for implementation, and interaction with state law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple cancellation mechanism must be easy to find
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a consumer enrolls online, sellers must afford an equally simple online cancellation experience, i.e., one that allows consumers easily to find and use the cancellation mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include a clearly-labeled cancellation link or button on a website or within a user's account or device settings. The mechanism need not be the exact same medium as consent but cannot be made more difficult to use or find than the consent mechanism. Sellers cannot prominently label the mechanism within account settings but make account settings hard to locate. The mechanism must be easy to find at the time the consumer decides to cancel; providing cancellation information only at enrollment does not discharge the obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancellation must be 'equally simple' in practical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Cancellation mechanisms must be as easy to use as the mechanism the consumer used to sign up in terms of time, expense, burden, and ease of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess parity across dimensions like time, cost, and user burden. Asymmetrical experiences (e.g., online sign-up but telephone-only cancellation with long hold times or onerous verification) create unreasonable barriers. Sellers should ensure cancellation does not require materially more effort or expense than enrollment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interactive electronic medium defined broadly
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rule's use of 'interactive electronic medium' includes all electronic communications (except telephone calls), covering chat, text, email, messaging, and other electronic media whether or not they strictly use the internet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This broad definition covers MMS/SMS, chat systems, and email; it provides flexibility while ensuring parallel sign-up and cancellation procedures meet consumer expectations. Sellers should treat these media as 'online' for cancellation-parity purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement to interact with live/virtual agent for online cancellation (unless consumer enrolled that way)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sellers may not require consumers to engage with a live or virtual agent to cancel when the consumer enrolled online, unless the consumer consented to the negative option feature through such an agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a consumer did not interact with an agent to enroll, imposing agent-mediated cancellation (phone, chat with rep, messaging that requires a rep) is prohibited. This prevents use of chat/text/messaging to recreate the abuses seen with telephone cancellation. Sellers that use agent-based enrollment may require agent interaction for cancellation only if the consumer did so at enrollment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancellation mechanisms cannot erect unreasonable barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Sellers must not create unreasonable hold times, verification requirements, aggressive 'save' tactics, or other tactics that impede immediate halting of charges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of unlawful barriers include extended hold times, requiring repeated identification steps beyond normal verification, forcing consumers through multiple upsells before cancellation, or making cancellation materially inconvenient or costly. Save attempts that require consumers to navigate upsells, jump through hoops, or wait unreasonable amounts of time violate the 'simple' requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telephone cancellation: prompt effectuation via answered or message-recording number
rubrics_metrics.description: Sellers must promptly effectuate cancellation requests by consumers via a telephone number that is answered or records messages during normal business hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sellers need not physically answer every call; an answering machine that clearly provides for cancellation (e.g., instructs callers to identify subscription and leave identifying information) is acceptable provided it is regularly monitored and cancellation requests are promptly effectuated. Sellers cannot limit telephone availability to hours so inconvenient they create a barrier (e.g., midnight–3 a.m.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Telephone cancellation cost parity
rubrics_metrics.description: Any cancellation call cannot be more expensive than the call used to enroll (e.g., if sign-up was toll-free, cancellation must be toll-free).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consumers would not expect to pay more to cancel than they did to enroll; charging higher call fees (or imposing other costs tied to cancellation) is unfair or deceptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: In-person sellers must provide non-in-person cancellation alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Sellers who obtain in-person consent must provide alternatives to in-person cancellation, either online or by phone, at the seller's choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The alternative must not impose costs that create an unreasonable barrier to cancellation. The Commission corrected prior language tying the alternative call cost to in-person consent cost and instead requires that the alternative not be unreasonably expensive. Sellers without any online presence may offer phone cancellation if they comply with telephone cancellation requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Email is an acceptable online cancellation medium
rubrics_metrics.description: The final Rule does not bar the use of email to effectuate online cancellation; several States specifically allow email as an online cancellation method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite some commenters' objections, the record provided no basis to prohibit email. When using email, sellers should ensure cancellation via email meets the 'simple' and prompt effectuation requirements and is as easy to use as enrollment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-factor and routine verification procedures are acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing verification procedures, such as two-factor authentication, are sufficient to ensure the correct person is cancelling and do not require a cancellation mechanism different than enrollment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sellers may use common authentication methods to confirm identity without forcing a more burdensome cancellation medium than enrollment required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saves (retention offers) not adopted as opt-in; cannot interfere with simple cancellation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission did not adopt the proposed provision requiring consumers to opt-in to receive 'saves' prior to cancellation, but emphasizes that save attempts that interfere with the requirement to provide a simple, easy-to-use cancellation mechanism are prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the opt-in saves proposal may have unintended consequences (e.g., thwarting confirmation of intent or blocking valuable concessions), it was deferred. However, sellers may not use saves to force consumers through upsells, long waits, or extra hoops that prevent reasonably immediate cancellation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual reminder proposal characteristics (under consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: The NPRM proposed requiring annual reminders for non-physical goods sold with a negative option feature, identifying the product/service, frequency and amount of charges, and means to cancel, delivered through the same medium the consumer used to consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was a proposed requirement (the Commission will seek more comment). Commenters suggested alternatives including opt-outs, varying frequency (e.g., every six months, before each charge), reminders at free-trial end, or letting consumers choose reminder medium. Sellers should note the Commission is considering scope (types of services, timing) and potential interplay with state reminder requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of material terms before charging required; no after-sale notice mandate
rubrics_metrics.description: The final Rule requires sellers to disclose important information prior to charging the consumer (§425.4), including all material terms such as range of costs and frequency of charges; the Commission did not require notice of material changes after sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to disclose material terms upfront clearly and conspicuously violates the Rule. Whether failure to notify of material changes is unfair or deceptive is fact-specific (e.g., significant unilateral short-term price hikes may be deceptive). Sellers should provide clear upfront disclosures; post-sale change notice is not mandated but may be required under state law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to State laws and preemption limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rule does not supersede, alter, or affect State statutes, regulations, orders, or interpretations relating to negative option marketing except to the extent a State provision is inconsistent with the Rule; State requirements that afford greater protection are not inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preemption is limited to situations where it is impossible to comply with both or where State law would frustrate the Rule's purposes. Sellers must comply with applicable State laws that provide equal or greater consumer protection. The Commission will maintain the ability of States to act as laboratories for consumer protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions process for sellers (new §425.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sellers and other covered persons may seek full or partial exemptions from the Rule if they can demonstrate that application of the Rule's requirements to a particular product, service, or class is not necessary to prevent the acts or practices to which the Rule relates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitions for exemption should follow the FTC's Rules of Practice and the procedures in §1.31. Exemptions are fact-dependent and evaluated on a case-by-case basis with supporting evidence and data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severability (new §425.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: The provisions of the final Rule are separate and severable; if a court finds any part of the Rule invalid, the remainder of the Rule remains in force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves enforceability of the Rule's other provisions if a specific provision is stayed or invalidated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation timeline and phased compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: The final Rule provides 180 days from publication for full compliance, but sellers must comply with §425.3 (prohibitions on misrepresentations in connection with a negative option feature) within 60 days of publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission recognizes implementation burdens and gave staggered deadlines. Sellers should prioritize compliance with misrepresentation prohibitions immediately (60 days) and plan system/process changes to be completed within 180 days. Existing federal and state laws and prior guidance may enable a head start on compliance.
